hints: Start by naming the two compartments in Fig. 6.1 - the large central matrix and the narrow intermembrane space - and recall in which direction protons are pumped using energy from the electron transport chain.
walkthrough:
Picture Where Protons Are Pumped**
Think of the inner membrane as a dam. During oxidative phosphorylation, energy from electrons is used to pump $H^+$ ions from the matrix, where they are low in concentration, up into the intermembrane space, where they become highly concentrated. That is active transport because it needs energy to move against the gradient.

Match Direction To The Arrows**
Arrow D starts in the matrix and points outward into the intermembrane space. That outward pumping direction is exactly the active transport of protons, so the answer is D.

hints: Recall where $CO_2$ is made in respiration and think about its concentration inside versus outside the mitochondrion, then look for arrows that move outward down that gradient without needing energy.
walkthrough:
Remember Where $CO_2$ Comes From**
$CO_2$ is released in the matrix by decarboxylation in the link reaction and the Krebs cycle. That means its concentration is highest in the matrix and lowest outside the mitochondrion.

Follow Diffusion Outward**
Diffusion always moves from high to low concentration and needs no ATP. Any arrow leaving the matrix to the outside and then leaving the mitochondrion shows this outward loss. Both D (matrix to intermembrane space) and C (out of the mitochondrion) show that outward diffusion path, so both are correct.

hints: Focus on the fluid centre of the mitochondrion and list which stages of aerobic respiration are located there rather than on the membranes.
Think about what the matrix contains for making its own proteins - DNA, ribosomes and enzymes - and why respiratory enzymes and carriers are needed there.
Link the products made in the matrix - reduced coenzymes and a small amount of ATP - to the next stage on the cristae.
walkthrough:
Home Of Link And Krebs**
The matrix is the aqueous centre where pyruvate is decarboxylated in the link reaction and acetyl CoA is fully oxidised in the Krebs cycle. Enzymes for both cycles are dissolved here, so this is where $CO_2$ is released and where most of the reduced coenzymes are made.

Factory For Its Own Machinery**
The matrix also has small circular mitochondrial DNA and 70S ribosomes. Together they make some of the proteins needed for respiration itself, such as enzymes for the Krebs cycle and protein electron carriers for the inner membrane.

Supply Line For Oxidative Phosphorylation**
The key output is reduced NAD and reduced FAD, which then carry hydrogen to the electron transport chain on the cristae. A little ATP is also made directly in the Krebs cycle by substrate-linked phosphorylation.

Final answer: Site of link reaction and Krebs cycle; produces reduced NAD and reduced FAD for oxidative phosphorylation; small ATP yield by substrate-linked phosphorylation; contains DNA and ribosomes to synthesise respiratory enzymes, coenzymes and electron carriers.

hints: Start at the end of the electron transport chain and recall the normal role of oxygen when electrons and $H^+$ arrive there.
Think through what happens to electron flow and $H^+$ pumping if that final acceptor is missing and electrons have nowhere to go.
Connect loss of $H^+$ pumping to the proton gradient between the intermembrane space and matrix and to movement through ATP synthase.
Consider the knock-on effect on the carriers NAD and FAD and on overall ATP yield if the chain backs up.
walkthrough:
Oxygen Is The Final Sink**
In normal oxidative phosphorylation, electrons pass along carriers in the inner membrane, releasing energy. At the very end, oxygen accepts the electrons and combines with $H^+$ to form water. Without oxygen there is no final acceptor, so electrons cannot leave the chain.

Chain Jams And Pumping Stops**
Because electrons cannot exit, they back up and stop entering and moving along the chain. The energy that normally pumps $H^+$ from the matrix into the intermembrane space is no longer released, so little or no $H^+$ is pumped and the steep proton (electrochemical) gradient collapses.

No Gradient Means No ATP**
ATP synthase makes ATP only when $H^+$ flow back down their gradient by chemiosmosis. With no or a weak gradient, chemiosmosis stops or slows greatly, so little or no ATP is made by oxidative phosphorylation.

Carriers Stay Reduced**
Reduced NAD and reduced FAD normally drop off hydrogen and become oxidised to NAD and FAD for reuse in glycolysis, link and Krebs. When the chain is blocked they stay reduced, so oxidised carriers are not recycled and the earlier stages also slow.

Final answer: Oxidative phosphorylation stops / decreases because: oxygen is the final electron acceptor so no / fewer electrons accepted; electrons stop moving along ETC; no / less $H^+$ pumped so no / reduced proton gradient; no / less chemiosmosis through ATP synthase; reduced NAD / FAD not oxidised so NAD / FAD not recycled; no / less ATP produced.
